jsnvu6-e181455-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 9: in what subject faith exists, referring to Aquinas.

jsnvu6-e181455-d1e115.summary: Argument that faith is not in the damned: we walk by faith (2 Cor. 5), but the damned have reached their term and walk no further.
claims: The damned, being at their term, lack faith (objection)

jsnvu6-e181455-d1e128.summary: Further arguments: faith is not in demons, since some hold that no good and praiseworthy act can be in demons, and believing God is such an act; nor in heretics, since an infused habit, like charity, is lost by a single contrary act, and every heretic has acts contrary to faith.
claims: Demons cannot have the praiseworthy act of faith (objection)
Heretics lose infused faith by a single contrary act (objection)

jsnvu6-e181455-d1e151.summary: Arguments for the opposite: if the damned lacked faith, damned believers would not differ from damned infidels; and James 1 [2] says demons believe and tremble, with a gloss on Romans calling their faith unformed.
claims: Damned believers differ from damned infidels by retaining faith
Demons believe and tremble

jsnvu6-e181455-d1e167.summary: Further argument for the opposite: one who errs about one object of science does not lose the whole science, so one who errs about one credible does not lose faith; this is the heretic's case.
claims: Error about one credible does not destroy the whole habit of faith

jsnvu6-e181455-d1e180.summary: The question concerns infused faith. Clear: unformed faith remains in all wayfarers who sin only against charity and good morals, because faith is given principally for the state of the way and such sins oppose charity, not faith. Doubtful: heretics, the damned generally, and demons specifically.
claims: The question concerns infused faith
Unformed faith remains in wayfarers who sin only against charity or morals
Faith is given principally for the state of the way

jsnvu6-e181455-d1e217.summary: On heretics: rejects the view that infused faith departs because it renders the intellect both ready to believe and discerning to reject error, which heretics lack. Every habit gives facility, not necessity, toward its act and against contraries, as with acquired habits. Moreover, one newly misled about a particular credible—by ignorance of Scripture or false teaching, e.g. that swearing is unlawful—assents to the other credibles exactly as before, and so by the same infused habit. Habit of faith and an erroneous act can coexist, as science can with an erroneous act; even a firmed false habit can coexist since its object differs. Thus faith probably remains in those newly erring about a particular credible.
claims: Habits give facility but not necessity, so error does not necessarily expel the habit
A newly misled heretic assents to other credibles by the same infused habit
Habitual faith and an erroneous act about one credible can coexist
Infused faith probably remains in heretics erring about a particular article

jsnvu6-e181455-d1e308.summary: On damned humans who die with faith but without grace: grace is irrecoverably absent, and hope cannot act, since they know beatitude is unattainable, and would remain in vain as a habit. But neither the habit nor the act of faith conflicts with their state; indeed, through the worm of conscience they are probably tormented over lacking the divine vision, known only by faith, and over not doing what faith prescribed. So faith remains in them in habit and in some acts.
claims: The damned lack grace and acts of hope
Faith remains in the damned in habit and some acts
The damned's torment of conscience presupposes faith

jsnvu6-e181455-d1e343.summary: On demons: answer depends on whether they had faith from creation. Some argue all angels had faith from the start since they were created in grace and among pure wayfarers there is no grace without faith (Heb. 11). If so, demons retain it: not lost by their state, since the damned keep faith and only the state of vision removes faith, nor by their act, since their sin was not against faith. Some reply that demons now assent because of evident signs, not divine authority, as when they confessed Christ the Son of God.
claims: If angels were created in grace, they had faith from the start
The state of obstinacy does not exclude faith; only vision does
The demons' sin was not against faith
Some say demons now assent from evident signs rather than divine authority

jsnvu6-e181455-d1e399.summary: Against that reply: signs and miracles do not remove faith but induce and confirm it, as Scripture shows repeatedly (Exodus 14; John 2, 10, 11, 15). So if demons had faith originally, Christ's signs did not take it away, at least in habit, though an assent based purely on seen signs would not be an act of faith, which requires divine authority. If demons lacked faith originally, it is not credible that it was later infused.
claims: Miracles induce and confirm faith rather than destroying it
Assent based purely on signs is not an act of faith, which rests on divine authority
If demons lacked faith originally, it was not later infused

jsnvu6-e181455-d1e449.summary: A not unreasonable alternative: the angels lacked faith from creation though created in grace. If it is evident that God has said something, it is known scientifically to be true, since God cannot lie, even without seeing the connection of terms; faith is then unnecessary. Any revelation to angels at creation could not come from man or from another angel without their perceiving it, so they would know that God revealed it, and would have science rather than faith. Thus the argument that grace requires faith does not compel.
claims: Evident knowledge that God has spoken yields science, not faith
Angels would have known that a revelation came from God
Angels may have lacked faith from creation

jsnvu6-e181455-d1e499.summary: Heb. 11 on the necessity of faith applies to human adults, for whom divine revelation is known only by believing. For angels, if anything was revealed, their merit lay not in believing but in obeying the divine precept (as in Book 2), just as Christ, without faith, merited by obedience unto death (Phil. 2).
claims: The necessity of faith for pleasing God applies to human adults
Angelic merit consisted in obedience, not belief
Christ merited by obedience without having faith

jsnvu6-e181455-d1e521.summary: Reply to the first argument: though faith is given principally for the way, it can remain at the term when nothing opposes it and it has some act there.
claims: Faith can remain at the term absent anything repugnant

jsnvu6-e181455-d1e537.summary: Reply to the second: some hold that a good and praiseworthy though non-meritorious act can be in demons, so their act of faith is possible; alternatively the demons' act of believing may be corrupted by some evil circumstance and so be bad.
claims: Demons may have good non-meritorious acts, or their belief may be vitiated by circumstance

jsnvu6-e181455-d1e553.summary: Reply to the third: grace is lost by a single mortal sin, but the habits of faith and hope need not be lost by a single contrary act—those who believe something contrary to Scripture out of ignorance retain faith, and one recovering from despair needs only a new act of hope, not a new habit. The first and third contrary arguments are conceded; James's statement about demons is read by some of infused faith, by others of credulity based on seen signs and miracles.
claims: Grace is lost by one mortal sin, but faith and hope are not lost by one contrary act
Ignorant error about Scripture does not remove the habit of faith
Recovery from despair requires a new act, not a new habit, of hope

jsnvu6-e181455.summary: Question 9 asks in which subjects infused faith exists. It is clear that unformed faith remains in wayfarers who sin only against charity or good morals, since faith is given chiefly for the way and such sins do not oppose it. The doubtful cases are heretics, the damned, and demons. Heretics newly misled about a particular credible probably retain infused faith: habits give facility, not necessity, and these heretics assent to the other articles as before, so habit and an erroneous act can coexist, as in science. The damned lose grace and the act of hope, but retain faith in habit and some acts, since faith underlies their torment of conscience. For demons there are two views. If angels were created with faith, demons keep it, since neither their state nor their sin excludes it and miracles confirm faith rather than destroy it. Alternatively, and not unreasonably, angels never had faith: any revelation they received would be evidently from God and so known scientifically, and their merit lay in obedience, as Christ merited without faith. Grace is lost by one mortal sin, but faith and hope are not lost by one contrary act.
claims: Unformed faith remains in wayfarers sinning against charity
Heretics newly erring about one article probably retain the habit of infused faith
The damned retain faith in habit and some acts, but lack grace and acts of hope
Whether demons have faith depends on whether angels had faith at creation; it is plausible they had science rather than faith
Faith and hope are not lost by a single contrary act, unlike grace
